content:
Thinking about "mathlib quality code", and the many deficiencies in current Mathlib, I would like to study how many "bad defeq problems" we have hiding behind exact calls in Mathlib.

I would like to investigate (possibly via a hook as described by Robin Arnez here) all the uses of exact in Mathlib today:

  1. Working out which work under with_reducible or with_reducible_and_instances, and which actually require unfolding default reducibility definitions
  2. Also measuring the wall-clock / heartbeats for all of these.

(It's probably valuable to do the same with apply and refine as well.)

This will tell us how much of a problem we have.

One potential solution to these problems would be to decide that exact is actually a low-level tactic, and should mostly be replaced by one of two tactics:

  1. identically X, which is just short-hand for with_reducible_and_instances exact X
  2. definitionally X, which is exact X, possibly with a (CI?) linter that ensures identically X doesn't work.

And perhaps we then record all the definitionally X in the technical debt report!

(Tongue in cheek, but if we went with those tactic names we should also make simply X a macro for simpa using X... :-)

I would welcome anything that allows us to programmatically identify and report defeq abuse, a topic which to my knowledge is pretty opaque in terms of documentation.

If using new versions of such a common tactic is a time consuming obstacle for this, could we make some immediately headway with a tactic analysis linter to report on the replacements you are proposing?

It's actually not quite as bad as I expected. Some highlights:

  • There are ~35,000 exact calls in Mathlib
  • Of these about 5,000 require default reducibility (the others work as reducible or instances)
  • The median heartbeat count for the "requires default transparency" population is about twice as high (similarly for wall-clock).
  • But there is actually more variation within the reducible transparency population:

That's more like what I was expecting:

  • Reducible calls: median isDefEq cost of just 54 heartbeats — nearly free
  • Default-only calls: median isDefEq cost of 3,985 heartbeats — 74x more expensive
Note this is only counting heartbeats inside isDefEq now.
It's a big difference between the two populations, but maybe the "bad" population is still not bad enough to warrant the tactic changes I proposed above. Happy to hear opinions on this.

Those are some nice plots, but i find it hard to read where all colors overlap versus just two...
Is there an obvious explanation for the two three green peaks?
I would be in favor of exactly X, definitionally X, and simply X.

I don't see the point of splitting exact. I think there are many cases where using semireducible defeq isn't actually code smell. Do we gain anything from splitting that we cannot gain from posting the above table on Zulip once a week/month?
Let's try to minimize the number of different tactics when it's not strictly necessary. Each new tactic is another thing to learn for newcomers.

Kim Morrison said:

Note this is only counting heartbeats inside isDefEq now.

Maybe not important, but I see 4 distinct colors in the graph, and none of them match the color of Instances...
I interpreted that as the three colors overlapping, with Instances at the bottom?

Also your comment about reporting is pretty much what I had in mind with

Chris Henson said:

...a tactic analysis linter to report on the replacements you are proposing

and is maybe how that graph was constructed in the first place?

Johan Commelin said:

I would be in favor of exactly X, definitionally X, and simply X.

If we change behaviour at all, i dont think this is the correct change. I think we should keep exact, but (if it is a large enough source of abuse) make it default to reducible transparency only, with a spelling like exact! for stronger reducibilities. Similarly for simpa. The reason why I think this is better is that the tactic is too ubiquitous to be renamed, and instead a behaviour change is more reasonable.

<rant>

Note that for the purposes of migrating, at first we would need to add an option backward.tactic.strictExact which enables this new behaviour, announce to the public in advance that the maintainers decided that mathlib will be changing to this standard and when the transition should be complete, and only after that deadline actually globally enable the strict behaviour for mathlib. Announcing this only in the nightly and reviewer channels is not enough.

So ideally it goes like:
- Lean adds new behaviour to exact which is disabled by default but can be enabled by an option, and publishes it in a RC.
- Mathlib maintainers announce publicly(!) that mathlib will aim to use the new behaviour globally by some concrete date. Uses of exactwithout the new behaviour are added to the tech debt counter.
- At the announced date, the new behaviour is globally enabled in mathlib. </rant>

Tldr: don't change the name of exact, instead add an option to make exact behave more strictly, which mathlib can gently migrate to, and I am still upset about how the backwards.isDefeq.respectTransparency change was handled (e.g. not publicly announced) and want the potential exact migration to be different.
Questions around communication aside, I like the idea of exact!.
I would much prefer keeping a single exact but having efficient tooling in CI telling us when it’s costly.

My problem in general is that it's really difficult to tell what level of transparency everything is happening at. It seems to change pretty arbitrarily (I've complained before about abbrev in this context). I think that it should be intuitive to understand how deeply Lean is unfolding a term.

Patrick Massot said:

I would much prefer keeping a single exact but having efficient tooling in CI telling us when it’s costly.

That helps for mathlib, but it's another bunch of setup work for any new project

I think it's very unlikely we will change the operation of exact in lean4. That's why I framed the above proposal as "thinking of exact as a low-level tactic, and adding behaviour on top of it".

Partly this is because ridiculously slow defeqs are a bit of a Mathlib specialty, and partly because this design space is big, and unclear what the best solution is, and some evidence from iterating within Mathlib first would be required before considering any language level changes.

Edward van de Meent said:

the tactic is too ubiquitous to be renamed

Yes, exact is certainly staying as is, with the with combinators: as above, the choice is about implementing things on top.

But on top I think "it's never too late" to make big changes!

Ruben Van de Velde said:

Patrick Massot said:

I would much prefer keeping a single exact but having efficient tooling in CI telling us when it’s costly.

That helps for mathlib, but it's another bunch of setup work for any new project

If it's packaged into a linter, I think this can be pretty easy. In CSLib for instance, we just copied over the workflow from Mathlib for the weekly linting. It was a very smooth process. In general, I think it is very valuable to encourage downstream repos to inherit these kinds of reports.
